suppressed.title: Load pets lazily and fetch them when needed
suppressed.summary: The eager one-to-many on `Owner.pets` can cause the owner query to drag in every pet collection even when the caller only needs owner fields.

suggestion.rationale: This lets JPA load the owner row first and only initialize the pets collection if application code actually accesses it, avoiding unnecessary collection loading for owner-only reads.
suggestion.equivalenceArgument: This is not equivalent: callers that previously received an initialized collection immediately may now trigger lazy initialization later, and code that depends on eager loading timing can behave differently; the returned owner and pet rows are the same when the collection is accessed, but loading behavior changes.
assumptions: Callers do not rely on `pets` being initialized outside a persistence context.
Any code that needs pets already loaded will fetch them explicitly or within an active session.
suggestion.expectedImpact: Avoids loading pet collections for owner reads that never touch `pets`, reducing database work to only the rows actually accessed.

evidence.quote:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS pets (
  id INT(4) UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(30),
  birth_date DATE,
  type_id INT(4) UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  owner_id INT(4) UNSIGNED,
  INDEX(name),
  FOREIGN KEY (owner_id) REFERENCES owners(id),
  FOREIGN KEY (type_id) REFERENCES types(id),
  UNIQUE (owner_id, name)
) engine=InnoDB;
evidence.relevance: The association is stored through `owner_id`, so fetching pets by owner benefits from an index on that join column.
The H2 schema also stores the relationship in `owner_id`, but only indexes `name`, so owner-based collection loading has no supporting index here.

groundingNotes: Redundant recommendation — The repository already declares an identical index (idx_pets_owner_id) at src/main/resources/db/postgres/schema.sql:44.
Reported as an N+1, but the query is not inside a loop in the fetched source. One of those is wrong, and only one of them was checked.

verified: Neither version orders its rows, so neither guarantees an order.
equivalence.summary: Verified (hibernate): every mechanically decidable property of the result is identical.

counted: Declares the association lazy, so the collection is no longer loaded with the parent on every read of that entity. (Counted from the mapping, not measured.)
unmeasured: Whether any caller iterates these parents and then touches the collection. If one does, lazy loading converts a single eager load into one query per parent — an N+1 introduced by this change. A fetch mode is a property of the mapping, so the callers are every place the entity is read, and source code cannot settle it.
Whether this is actually faster. speeDB does not execute anything — it has no connection, no timings and no query plan.
Whether an equivalent index already exists in production. Migration files record intent, not the live schema.
The write cost of the new index, which is paid on every insert and update to the table.

suppressed.title: Delay loading visits until accessed
suppressed.summary: The eager one-to-many on `visits` can trigger extra database work whenever a `Pet` is loaded, even if the caller never needs the collection.

suggestion.rationale: Lazy loading avoids fetching visit rows for every pet load and only issues SQL when code actually traverses the collection.
suggestion.equivalenceArgument: This is not equivalent: it changes when the `visits` rows are loaded and can change when lazy-loading exceptions occur, but it preserves the same rows, columns, ordering, NULL handling, and duplicates for callers that access the collection.
assumptions: Callers that need visits will access the collection within an open persistence context or otherwise load them explicitly.
`Visit` is mapped so that lazy loading is supported by the JPA provider.
suggestion.expectedImpact: Avoids an automatic collection load on every `Pet` fetch; visit rows are read only on demand.

evidence.relevance: This mapping forces eager collection loading for every `Pet` instance.

evidence.quote:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS visits (
  id INT(4) UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  pet_id INT(4) UNSIGNED,
  visit_date DATE,
  description VARCHAR(255),
  FOREIGN KEY (pet_id) REFERENCES pets(id)
) engine=InnoDB;
evidence.relevance: The visits table is separate and linked by `pet_id`, so loading it eagerly adds extra database work.
The H2 schema also models visits as a separate table joined by `pet_id`, reinforcing that eager loading can add extra reads.

suppressed.title: Load specialties lazily
suppressed.summary: The eager many-to-many mapping forces specialty rows to be loaded whenever a Vet is fetched, even if the caller never uses them.

suggestion.rationale: This defers loading the specialties collection until code actually accesses it, so a plain Vet fetch does not also materialize the join table and specialty entities.
suggestion.equivalenceArgument: This is not equivalent: it changes when related rows are loaded and can change the number of SQL statements, proxy behavior, and failure timing for detached access; the returned Vet columns and rows are unchanged, but persistence behavior is different.
assumptions: Callers that need specialties access them within an open persistence context, or are otherwise adapted to handle lazy loading.
suggestion.expectedImpact: Avoids loading the specialties association on every Vet read; related rows are fetched only on demand.

evidence.relevance: Shows the association is configured for eager loading through the join table.

evidence.quote:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS vet_specialties (
  vet_id INT(4) UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  specialty_id INT(4) UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (vet_id) REFERENCES vets(id),
  FOREIGN KEY (specialty_id) REFERENCES specialties(id),
  UNIQUE (vet_id,specialty_id)
) engine=InnoDB;
evidence.relevance: Confirms the association is backed by a join table and foreign-key lookups.
Confirms the same join-table shape in the H2 schema.

eager visits collection risks extra queries

declined.why: The issue is not an N+1 pattern from iteration over many pets; it is eager collection loading on a separate table, so I classified it as behavioural rather than an equivalent round-trip fix.
The eager association is a real performance concern, but changing it to lazy is behavioural rather than equivalent because it alters loading semantics and can change error timing.

unknowable: Row counts — no table size is recoverable from source.
Which indexes actually exist in production, versus which were declared in a migration that may have been superseded, reverted, or never run.
